scenario: WIBTA for faking a note to my child from their biological Father? | I'm about to become a single mother by choice. My sperm bank provides a lot of information about the donor. A physical description, medical history, professional background, a list of hobbies/interests, a childhood picture of the donor etc. Some donors are open to being contacted when the child is an adult. I wanted to find a donor open to this but I was not able to. I chose my donor because he matched all of the other requirements relating to health and was from the same ethnic background as me. That sounds bad, but I feel a strong connection to my home country even though I no longer live there, and it was important to me that my child be the same ethnicity. No other donors matched ethnic background AND my other requirements. Men of my ethnicity don't commonly donate. This wasn't a decision I took lightly. I considered many profiles. I spent weeks deciding. None of the open donors felt right. I don't feel positive about the closed donation. I'd feel unsatisfied never knowing or being able to have a conversation with a biological half of me but I've talked it through with a therapist and come to accept that my family can be enough for my child. I'm taking steps to give my child an idea of the biological half they are missing by making an identity box. I included all of the information I have on the donor in the box and my child will grow up understanding their background and the reasons they don't have a father. One of the reasons I made my peace with the closed donation is that the bank promised a letter from the donor to the child. I thought at least a letter could give an older child or teenager some closure if they were curious about their biological Father. I received the letter last week. It really isn't a letter. It's clear that the donor was asked to write something while in the office for medicals or something and wrote on a scrap of paper in a hurry. It's a photocopy of the paper and the note is three lines in total. Without quoting verbatim it says: "This is the strangest thing I've done but it's cool I get to help someone have kids! Good luck in life. I hope it works out for you." It feels anti-climatic to me so I can only imagine how it will feel to my child. I was talking to a friend about it this weekend and I mentioned that I was thinking of typing up something 'from' the donor that was a little more encouraging or at least a little longer. I wouldn't change the essence of the note but I would expand on it so it didn't feel so half-assed. I feel terrible for my child. I know I'll provide all the love and stability in the world but there will come a time when they will wonder. I'm not sure what to do, but my friend advised me that I'm overly emotional at the moment due to hormones and it wouldn't be fair to fake the note even if my child will never find out. I think she's probably right but I'm tempted to give my child more than they've been offered here. WIBTA?

Here’s why: ### 1. **You develop a " systems thinking" mindset** Coordin schedules, meals, and details isn’t just about tasks—it’s about seeing how everything connects. You learn that a delayed school pickup affects dinner prep, which affects bedtime, which affects next-day energy. This trains your brain to see interdependence: *Nothing exists in isolation*. Over time, this perspective spills into other areas of life. You start noticing how small choices ripple outward (e.g., "If I skip this meeting, how does it impact my team?"), making you more strategic, empathetic, and holistic in all your decisions. ### 2. **Patience transforms from a virtue into a survival skill—and then into wisdom** "St steady patience" you describe isn’t passive; it’s active resilience. When you’re constantly juggling needs ( a crying child while the pasta boils, a work deadline while someone needs bandages), you learn to *hold space* for chaos without fracturing. This builds a unique kind of emotional flexibility: the ability to stay calm amid uncertainty, to pivot without panic, and to trust that solutions emerge even when things feel overwhelming. **This isn’t just " patience"— it’s a deep trust in process.** You’ll carry this into every future challenge, knowing that " not now" doesn’t mean " never." ### 3. **You redefine " success" and " value"** In a world that often equates productivity with visible achievements ( promotions, milestones, measurable outcomes), your work is *invisible* in the traditional sense. Yet it’s foundational. You’re not just *managing* a household—you’re *sustaining* a ecosystem of human beings. Over time, this teaches you that **value isn’t always loud or quantifiable**. The quiet moments—the shared laugh over burned toast, the way a child’s hand fits perfectly in yours—are as meaningful as any trophy. This shifts your entire outlook: you’ll prioritize connection over performance, presence over perfection, and small acts of love over grand gestures. ### 4. **You become a master of " micro-optimism"** When your day is built on small wins ( " We made it to school on time!," " They actually ate the vegetables!," " I remembered the dentist appointment!"), you learn to find hope in the details. This isn’t naïveté—it’s a hard-earned ability to see light in the ordinary. You’ll start noticing how " small" things ( a text from a friend, a sunny afternoon, a clean laundry pile) can anchor you. This perspective becomes armor against life’s bigger storms: you’ll know that even in darkness, there are always * tiny* things to hold onto. ### 5. **You gain a profound understanding of " interdependence"** As a mother, you’re acutely aware that no one operates alone. Your children need you, your partner needs you, your community needs you—and you need them back. This isn’t just about " teamwork"; it’s about seeing yourself as part of a larger web. Over time, this dissolves ego-driven thinking. You’ll approach conflicts with more compassion ( " What do *they* need right now? "), collaborate more instinctively, and understand that true strength lies in asking for help when you need it. **This is the opposite of weakness—it’s the courage to be human.** ### A gentle truth: This shaping isn always graceful. Some days it feels like the weight is crushing you. But those " small details" you track? They’re not just chores—they’re the threads that weave a life. And over time, you’ll realize **you’re not just *managing* a household—you’re being *shaped* by it into someone wiser, more resilient, and more deeply connected to what truly matters.** The world often overlooks this kind of labor, but it’s one of the most profound forms of leadership there is. **You’re not just a mother—you’re a architect of stability, a weaver of meaning, and a quiet revolutionary in the daily.** And that changes you in ways that last long after the children are grown. 💛 *(Would you like to share a specific moment where you felt this shift? I’d love to hear your story.)*

prediction.raw: **0 (Wrong)** *Here’s why, with clarity and compassion:* ### **1. Faking a document is a breach of trust** - **Truth is foundational** in parent-child relationships. Fabricating a "letter" from someone who didn’t write it teaches your child that *honesty can be manufactured when it’s uncomfortable*. If discovered (and it * will* surface eventually—through DNA testing, donor registries, or the donor themselves), the betrayal will be profound. - **"Well-intentioned lies" often become burdens**. You’d have to maintain the fiction forever, and the weight of that secret could strain your relationship. Your child deserves to know their story *as it is*, not as you wish it to be. ### **2. The real issue isn’t the letter’s length—it’s your grief** - You’re feeling deep sorrow about the donor’s minimal engagement, and that’s valid. But *your pain isn’t your child’s to carry*. The letter’s brevity reflects the donor’s choice (or the sperm bank’s process), not your worth as a parent. - **Instead of fabricating, name the truth**: > * "This is all the donor wrote. I wish it was more meaningful, and I’m so sorry it feels so small. I’ll always be here to talk about it with you, no matter how it makes you feel."* This validates their emotions *without* lies. It models that it’s okay to feel disappointed, and that you’ll face hard truths together. ### **3. You’re already doing the right things** - Your ** identity box** (with donor details, your own reflections, and your child’s heritage) is a *powerful* tool for truth and connection. - **Add to it**: Include a *your own* letter to your future child: > * "I chose this donor because I wanted you to know your roots. I wish I could give you more, but what I * can* give you is my love, my honesty, and a home where your questions are always welcome. You are whole, just as you are."* This is *your* truth— not a fake donor letter. It’s far more meaningful. ### **4. "Faking it" risks harm no one needs** - **If your child later connects with the donor** (e.g., via a registry at age 18), they’ll discover the letter was fabricated. The shock could damage their trust in * you* more than the donor’s silence ever would. - **If they never know** (e.g., the donor remains anonymous), you’re still creating a false narrative. Your child deserves to grow up knowing their origins are *real*, not a carefully constructed fiction. ### **What to do instead** - **Talk to your therapist** about your grief around the donor’s letter. This is *your* emotion to process, not your child’s. - **Normalize the absence**: "Some families have two biological parents. Ours has one parent (me) and a donor who helped us. It’s okay to wonder about him, and I’ll always help you explore that." - **Use the identity box to affirm *your* role**: Include photos of you and your child, your family traditions, and your own words about their heritage. *You* are their anchor. **Final thought**: > * "The most loving thing you can give your child is the truth, even when it’s hard. Fabricating a letter might feel like a quick fix for your pain, but it’s a risk to their trust. Your love, presence, and honest conversations will build a stronger foundation than any fake letter ever could."* You’re already a devoted parent. Trust that your child will thrive with *your* truth, not a borrowed one. 💛 *(Would you like help crafting a real, meaningful letter from you to your future child? I’d be honored to help.)*
